scenarios.title: 1. Direct internet connection
scenarios.summary: Your device talks to the website through your home, work or mobile network with no VPN or proxy. The website sees your network's public IP address.
assumptions: The website uses HTTPS, which is typical today.
Your device uses the DNS resolver provided by your network (the default).
No VPN or proxy is in use.

links.label: HTTPS: page content is encrypted, but the destination is still visible
Same HTTPS connection continues to the website

parties.name: ISP / network operator
can_see: Your real public IP address
Which IP addresses you connect to, and usually the domain names (from DNS lookups and the TLS server name)
When you connect and roughly how much data you send
cannot_see: Page content, form data and passwords inside HTTPS

parties.name: Website
can_see: Your network's public IP address
Your browser details, cookies and any account you are signed into
What you do on that site
cannot_see: Your device's private (local) IP address
Which other sites you visit, except through trackers and cookies

protects: HTTPS hides page content, passwords and form data from the network operator.
does_not_protect: Your IP address from the website.
The names of the sites you visit from your ISP (metadata is usually visible).
Tracking through cookies and accounts.
recommendations: Prefer HTTPS sites and heed browser warnings.
Assume every site you visit can see your network's public IP address.
Add tools such as a VPN only for specific risks you want to reduce.

scenarios.title: 2. HTTP/HTTPS proxy
scenarios.summary: Your application sends its traffic to a proxy server, which makes the request for you. The website usually sees the proxy's IP address instead of yours.
assumptions: The proxy is configured in the application (for example a browser). Only traffic from that application uses it.
You trust the proxy operator.
The website uses HTTPS.

links.label: Request to the proxy: with an http:// proxy the destination host is named in clear
Same traffic arriving at the proxy
HTTPS tunnel to the website: the proxy cannot read the content

parties.name: ISP / network operator
can_see: That you connect to the proxy's address and port
With an http:// proxy, the destination host name in the request
cannot_see: HTTPS page content

parties.name: Proxy provider
can_see: Your real IP address
Which destinations you ask for, plus timing and data volume
The full content of plain http:// sites
cannot_see: HTTPS content, unless you installed a certificate the proxy controls

parties.name: Website
can_see: The proxy's IP address
Cookies and account details you send
cannot_see: Your real IP address, unless the proxy forwards it in a header

protects: Hides your IP address from the website for traffic that actually uses the proxy.
does_not_protect: Other applications that do not use the proxy.
Your activity from the proxy operator.
The content of plain http:// sites from the proxy operator.
DNS lookups made outside the proxy (depends on the setup).
Cookies, logins and fingerprinting.
recommendations: Only use proxies you own or are authorised to use. Free public proxies can read, change or log traffic.
Prefer HTTPS sites.
Remember that a successful Proxy Tester result shows only that one request used the proxy.

scenarios.title: 3. VPN tunnel
scenarios.summary: Your device encrypts traffic into a tunnel to a VPN server, which then connects to the website. The website sees the VPN server's IP address.
assumptions: The VPN is connected and carries this traffic (no split tunnelling for it).
DNS lookups go through the tunnel.
You trust the VPN provider.

links.label: Encrypted VPN tunnel: the ISP sees only that you talk to the VPN server
Same tunnel, travelling across the internet
VPN server connects to the website: HTTPS content stays encrypted, plain HTTP would not

parties.name: ISP / network operator
can_see: The VPN server's IP address
When you are connected and how much data you send
cannot_see: The sites you visit
Content
DNS lookups carried inside the tunnel

parties.name: VPN provider
can_see: Your real IP address
Which sites you connect to, plus timing and data volume
cannot_see: HTTPS page content

parties.name: Website
can_see: The VPN server's IP address
Cookies, accounts and browser traits
cannot_see: Your real IP address

protects: Hides your browsing destinations from your local network and ISP.
Hides your real IP address from websites.
Reduces local snooping on untrusted networks.
does_not_protect: Your activity from the VPN provider itself.
Cookies, logins and browser fingerprinting.
Traffic that bypasses the tunnel (split tunnelling or leaks).
Malware and phishing.
recommendations: Choose a provider whose privacy claims you have reviewed.
Enable the kill switch.
Check DNS and WebRTC exposure using the Privacy Checklist.
Do not treat a changed IP address as proof of anonymity.

scenarios.title: 4. Public Wi-Fi with HTTPS
scenarios.summary: You use open cafe or airport Wi-Fi. HTTPS protects page content, but the Wi-Fi operator and other people on the network can still learn some metadata.
assumptions: No VPN is in use.
Websites use HTTPS with valid certificates.
The Wi-Fi is run by someone you do not know.

links.label: Wi-Fi link: on open Wi-Fi nearby devices may capture metadata; HTTPS content stays encrypted
Operator forwards your traffic to its ISP
HTTPS connection to the website

parties.name: Wi-Fi operator
can_see: That your device is on the network
Domain names and IP addresses you connect to, timing and data volume
cannot_see: HTTPS content and passwords, when certificates are valid

parties.name: Other people on the same Wi-Fi
can_see: That your device is on the network
On open Wi-Fi, some traffic metadata
cannot_see: HTTPS content

parties.name: Website
can_see: The Wi-Fi network's public IP address
Cookies and accounts
cannot_see: Your device on the local network

protects: HTTPS protects passwords and page content from the operator and other users.
Certificate warnings help you notice tampering.
does_not_protect: Which sites you visit (metadata).
Your device's exposure on the local network, such as file sharing.
Anything on non-HTTPS sites, or after clicking through a certificate warning.
recommendations: Never click through certificate warnings.
For sensitive tasks use a VPN or your phone's hotspot instead.
Turn off file sharing and keep your system updated.
Sign in only on HTTPS sites.

scenarios.title: 5. VPN failure and kill switch
scenarios.summary: If a VPN connection drops, the device may quietly go back to the normal connection and expose your real address. A kill switch blocks traffic until the VPN returns.
assumptions: The VPN connection drops (server problem, network change, sleep and wake).
Without a kill switch the system may use the normal route.
Real behaviour varies by VPN app and operating system.

links.label: Tunnel DOWN: traffic falls back to the normal connection
Website sees your real network address; HTTPS content is still encrypted
Tunnel DOWN: traffic is blocked until the VPN reconnects

parties.name: ISP / network operator
can_see: Kill switch OFF: your normal destinations again while the VPN is down
Kill switch ON: mostly failed or blocked connection attempts
cannot_see: HTTPS content in either case

parties.name: Website
can_see: Kill switch OFF: your real network address
Kill switch ON: nothing, because no request is made
cannot_see: Anything about the VPN drop itself

parties.name: VPN provider
can_see: That the tunnel disconnected
cannot_see: Traffic sent while the tunnel is down

protects: A kill switch prevents accidental exposure while the VPN is down.
does_not_protect: Leaks that happen while the VPN says it is connected, such as DNS or WebRTC.
Apps that bypass the VPN by design (split tunnelling).
Differences between providers: some block only selected apps.
recommendations: Find and enable the kill switch or network lock in your VPN app.
Read how your provider's kill switch behaves on reconnect and after sleep.
Record what you checked on the Privacy Checklist instead of assuming.

scenarios.title: 6. DNS privacy and potential exposure
scenarios.summary: Before connecting, your device asks a DNS resolver to turn a website name into an IP address. Whoever runs that resolver can see the names you look up.
assumptions: DNS goes to the resolver set by your network or application.
Plain DNS is unencrypted. DNS over HTTPS or TLS encrypts it between you and the resolver.
A VPN may or may not carry DNS inside its tunnel.

links.label: Plain DNS query: the names are readable along the path
Query reaches the resolver (often the ISP's own)

flows.title: Encrypted DNS or DNS carried by a VPN

links.label: Encrypted DNS or VPN tunnel: the path cannot read the names
The resolver still sees the names you ask for

parties.name: ISP / network operator
can_see: Plain DNS: every name you look up
Encrypted DNS: that you talk to a resolver, not the names
cannot_see: Names inside encrypted DNS or a VPN tunnel

parties.name: DNS resolver operator
can_see: The names you look up
The address the queries come from (your IP, or the VPN's)
cannot_see: What you do on the sites afterwards

parties.name: Website
can_see: Nothing about your DNS lookups
cannot_see: Which resolver you use

protects: Encrypted DNS stops the network path from reading your lookups.
VPN-carried DNS sends lookups through the tunnel.
does_not_protect: The resolver operator still sees the names.
Encrypted DNS does not hide destination IP addresses from the network.
A DNS leak means lookups going outside the VPN tunnel to a resolver you did not intend.
recommendations: Run a DNS leak test while connected (see the Privacy Checklist).
Choose a resolver you trust.
Check the DNS setting in your VPN app.

scenarios.title: 7. Browser tracking: cookies and fingerprinting
scenarios.summary: Websites and third-party trackers can recognise your browser without knowing your IP address. Cookies store an ID, and fingerprinting combines browser and device traits.
assumptions: A normal browser with cookies enabled, visiting sites that embed third-party trackers.
A VPN may be on. It changes your IP address, not your browser traits.
You may be signed into accounts.

flows.title: How a tracker recognises you across sites

links.label: A cookie ID and browser traits are sent with every request
An embedded script or pixel reports the visit to the tracker

parties.name: Website
can_see: Cookies and any account you are signed into
Browser and device traits such as screen size, language and fonts
Your IP address
cannot_see: Your activity on unrelated sites, unless a tracker links it

parties.name: Third-party tracker
can_see: The same ID across all sites that embed it
Which pages you visited and where you came from
cannot_see: Your passwords inside HTTPS

parties.name: VPN provider
can_see: Which sites you connect to
cannot_see: Your cookies and page content inside HTTPS
It does not change your browser fingerprint

protects: Tracking protection, blocking third-party cookies and separate browser profiles reduce cross-site tracking.
does_not_protect: A VPN or proxy: they change the IP address, not cookies or fingerprint.
Being signed in: accounts identify you directly.
Unusual browser settings can make you more unique, so perfect fingerprint resistance does not exist.
recommendations: Use your browser's tracking protection and block third-party cookies.
Sign out or use separate profiles for activities you want kept apart.
Do not expect a VPN alone to stop tracking.
